Knock an animal unconscious

Babysit it for three real-life hours

Get killed by a mosquito the size of a Honda Civic

Lose everything

Too hot? You’re dying.
Too cold? You’re dying.

A tribe that’s been playing since 2016 and owns the entire map

You tame one dodo.
Then a raptor.
Then suddenly you’re running a prehistoric real estate empire and haven’t slept in 3 days.

Final Verdict:
🦖 Beautiful
🔥 Stressful
💀 Lethal

Arc Raiders is a rare breed of game. A common theme following the looter/extraction genre and yet it brings to the table a few things that most developers currently cannot. Above average quality across the board from the launch. Legit. 

The graphics are solid and the production design on the levels is fantastic. The AI intelligence is dangerous, hard and annoying, presenting some real challenge to initially get used to and still fully capable of ending a good run real fast if you don't respect the threat. 

The game has its own style of future that fits well and looks good. Character creation is limited, There are real money outfits but also a whole host of free and obtainable options too so you can find some style you like. 

There are bugs in the game but they are constantly trying to be ironed out, as is the whole package. We have seen a few dire bugs (wall glitches mostly) that have been rectified and a couple of balance changes here and there, so I expect a couple more to come.

Now my biggest fear for this game was the 3rd person shooting (yes there are corner peeks, the camping is hard and pushing takes a little getting used to) but the fighting across different maps can still be tactful, strategic and a lot of fun. They have a decent selection of weaponry which can be very slightly improved with levelling up using materials and a basic selection of attachments.

There is a basic base to build up, some workbenches to construct and level and then blue prints that must be found and extracted in raid for pretty much all the gear, explosives and weapons in the game. There is a seasonal reset that you have to choose to go for and complete some pretty annoying tasks to achieve it. One of my biggest gripes currently is the inventory management, with limited storage space and so much crap and goop to hold, despite the numerous upgrades, you run out quick.

The funniest part of the game for me has been the interactions with other players along my Arc Raiders career and I can only express my thanks and gratitude to the players I randomly met and shared some crazy games with. There are a LOT of people that think this is a friendly game, and to a large extent, it can be thanks to the basic voice lines your player can shout as well as using your mic to talk out loud, but if you play the passive role, you will die many times to the more aggressive and greedy players.
I cannot express this more clearly:
The game is PvPvE. 
Solo's play with solo's, duo's play with duos and trio's play with trios, but the 2's and 3's are non stop gun fights 99% of the time. 
Solo's is... very mixed bag. Some days the whole server will come together to bring down the biggest machines in the game to achieve victory together, then other days you will be non stop camped, betrayed, or simply lose fights to other people or the AI. If you are not prepared to let go of what you have, don't bother playing, it will only sour your soul.

TLDR: Fucking good quality all around game. Props for actually putting something out that really felt crafted and cared for. Also way more fun than I expected from a 3rd person looter/shooter. I hope to see you top side Raider.

The perfect "middle ground" extraction shooter
If you love the idea of extraction shooters but find games like Escape from Tarkov too hardcore or punishing, Arc Raiders is exactly what you’ve been looking for. It captures that high-stakes tension without the overwhelming complexity.

Accessible Gameplay: It strikes a great balance—tense enough to keep your heart racing, but intuitive enough that you aren't spending hours in menus.
Helpful Community: The player base is surprisingly refreshing. While there is still plenty of PvP, you’ll often run into other players who are actually willing to team up or help you out during a tough run.
Responsive Devs: Embark Studios has been great so far. The game is already quite polished with minimal bugs, and when issues do pop up, the developers are quick to communicate and roll out hotfixes. 
Verdict:
It’s a blast to play right now, and I’m genuinely excited to see how the finished product evolves. Highly recommended for anyone wanting a smoother, more social extraction experience.

Solo play in ARC Raiders is excellent. It’s focused, tense, and atmospheric, but what really elevates it is the social experience—most players you run into while solo are surprisingly friendly and supportive over VOIP. Encounters feel intentional, communication is often respectful or cooperative, and the game rewards patience, awareness, and smart disengagement. It’s one of the strongest—and most human—solo experiences in the extraction space.

Duos & Trios turn the social layer into a cesspool—not because of your squad, but because of the other players. Proximity voice chat becomes a stage. Opposing teams talk to be heard, not to communicate—posturing, trash talk, and performative “cool guy” lines meant more for their friends than the fight itself.

ARC Raiders is a 10/10 game if you can tune out the worst parts of proximity VOIP. The core design is rock solid—combat, atmosphere, and extraction tension all work exactly as intended—but player VOIP frequently devolves into slurs and posturing that the game itself doesn’t meaningfully curb. It’s especially jarring in a title where the developers are clearly capable of sophisticated AI voice filtering, yet leave moderation of player hate-speech almost entirely unchecked.

Baldur's Gate 3 isn't just a game. It's an experience.

A story that you create. Most games give you the illusion of choice. Here, choices are real, and sometimes they hurt like hell. They're companions with souls. Whether it's the tragedy of Karlach, the fanaticism and subsequent development of Lae'zel, or the moral dilemmas with the Emperor and Orpheus - this game makes you feel something for them.

Gameplay? Pure freedom. As a Paladin, I expected to just "tank." Instead, I was given a playground where the only limit is my imagination. Do you want to talk an enemy into killing himself? That's possible. Do you want to throw him into a chasm? That's possible. Do you want to throw a bear at him? That's possible too. The system is complex, but incredibly rewarding. Every fight is a puzzle that you can solve with brute force (Divine Smite!), or cleverness.

Technical condition and visuals Graphics, character facial expressions and dubbing are on the level of the most expensive films. When a character talks to you, you believe every word. The music (Borislav Slavov) is a chapter in itself - goosebumps during boss fights are guaranteed.

I entered the world of Baldur's Gate as a skeptic. I leave as a fan who feels empty because it's over. Larian Studios has created a masterpiece that has set the bar so high that no one will surpass it for a long time.

If you're hesitating because "turn-based games aren't your thing" - give it a chance. It's quite possible that you'll discover your new favorite game. Just like me.

Baldur’s Gate 3 feels like a game that was created with the deliberate goal of becoming a masterwork, and it succeeds. It is not just a great RPG for its time. It is the kind of experience that will be referenced years from now when people talk about what the genre is capable of at its best. Every system, from storytelling to combat, feels intentional rather than filler.

What truly sets BG3 apart is the sheer freedom in its dialogue and decision making. Your choices do not just tweak minor outcomes. They shape relationships, alter entire story paths, and can fundamentally change how the world reacts to you. It genuinely feels like your story, not one you are passively moving through. The characters feel alive, the conversations feel natural, and more often than not, you find yourself pausing just to think about what you would actually say or do in that moment.

For anyone wondering whether Baldur’s Gate 3 is still worth playing in 2026, the answer is an easy yes. Skipping it would mean missing out on a once in a generation work of art. This is the kind of RPG that reminds you why the genre exists in the first place. Deep role playing, meaningful consequences, and a world that respects your intelligence as a player. I would absolutely recommend it to anyone searching for a truly one of a kind RPG experience.

First off: I haven’t played POE1, I have no baseline for how easy or hard POE2 is in comparison.
The only thing I do know is, that the game feels fun for most of the leveling/campaign experience. Notice how I wrote „most of“. Here’s a few points that bother me so much that they in my opinion value a negative review:
- the game sometimes feels unfair. Not talking about getting killed because of stupid mistakes, no, the game flat out kills you because you don’t have any more health or mana potions left.
- some bosses are a joke with some builds, close to unbeatable on others.
- loot feels rewarding, but the lack of tooltip explanations for what’s permanent, what removes something, how something interacts feels bad when you figure that out by „accident“
- isn’t POE2 supposed to be for a broader audience? I felt like this really didn’t hit the mark at some points. It feels intuitive from time to time, tutorials are nice and all, but some key mechanics, some interactions won’t be explained to you
- figuring stuff out on your own is impossible with the relatively high respec cost, the time investment and the expensive currency costs to get a build rolling
- there‘s not really any build variety and the game (as stated above) doesn’t encourage you to try stuff. It’s just way to punishing to do so.
- it’s kinda mandatory to at least invest into some stash tabs (which is fine). This is more of an information than it is a critique about the game. Every game needs to make money, they chose this route and I’m good with that. Just keep this in mind, when you decide to start playing.

DayZ isn't a game about zombies, now you might think that with the amount of time you spend in the game avoiding or killing geeks; but that's not at all where the game is. DayZ is at the core a survival simulator, it's a game that tests the border between social and selfish survival stratagem, what junction will you switch from being a reasonable man to a survivalist or a predator. DayZ is a place where we get to witness game theory at work, where finite resources and hurt feeling gradually tear away at our pragmatic approach, where generosity gets used and laughed at by cannibals wearing wolf pelts and a landscape oozing with the sickness of men, not the prion disease; the nature of war.

ARMA shows you the formal acts of warfare, it shows you what the tribe is capable of at scale in the application of violence, but it's abstracted. DayZ shows you what war actually is, strife, struggle, want, greed, desperation, the instincts that served us in nature rearing it's ugly head to violate the honor of civilized men. War isn't a tank rolling down your street, it isn't the bomb that blew up your church, war isn't the spear breaking upon the phalanx. War is you, war is the exigency of all organic life, we don't go to war we're born into it.

Only in offering a name to the demon have we wrongly divorced it from ourselves..

"Warfare is that thing that happens on television"

"War is what they talk about on the news"

Wrong, try DayZ and watch in real time a true simulation of what the entropy of trust looks like, when the game becomes so contaminated that the equilibrium has become mutual distrust and selfishness.

As a real HGV class 1 driver speaking from first hand experience this game is about the closest you're going to get to the real thing, I've been playing ETS2 for well over 10 years with nearly 1000 hours gameplay logged and I still come back to this game especially after new major updates are released. That brings me on to my next point, this game is now just over 13 years old and SCS still continue to keep this game updated with new gameplay mechanics, features, DLC and free of bugs; something not many developers tend to do, especially years after the original release date.

The game features nearly all European countries through the base game and through DLC as well as all the major truck manufacturers found across Europe which are Scania, Volvo, DAF, Mercedes, Renault, MAN and Iveco both in left and right hand drive. The game also features different types of trailers allowing you to pull a variety of cargo. Trucks and trailers (Which can be purchased using in game currency) can be fully modified both mechanically and cosmetically allowing you to drive your dream truck exactly how you want it.

You start as an employed driver working for companies until you make enough profit to purchase your own truck where you can then build your own company going at it either solo or as a team using AI drivers to increase your profit margins, however you want to play it's completely up to you.

I highly recommend playing with a steering wheel and pedals (And a H shifter if driving a manual transmission) as it allows you to have complete precise control of the truck compared to using a keyboard and mouse. I use a Logitech G920 which does a fantastic job especially for the fairly low cost to buy it, there are also dedicated truck wheels available to buy although these are much more expensive. I also use a TrackIR 5 with the track clip pro attached to my headphones for precise hands free camera control so I can look in both mirrors using just my head as you would do in a real truck, it all adds to the realism.

If you're thinking about buying this game then I definitely recommend it, it's a 10/10 from me!

Took about thirty hours for the game to click with me, and once it did I was able to really get into it. The game unfortunately feels like the core systems for three different games were cut out and glued together, which can occasionally lead to really fun gameplay, but more often than not results in tedium. 

Despite this, I really appreciate how the game innovates upon the loop from Fallouts 4 and 76. Where those two games slowly pushed for more survival-lite mechanics, Starfield introduces optional systems for hunger and status effects that can enhance gameplay pressures, and lead players to engage with the cooking and pharmaceutical crafting systems that were previously easy to overlook. 

The weapon customization sees a handful of improvements over previous titles, with the recon scope being much more useful, and its effect being available on scopeless weapons via a new laser sight. The only real setback in the weapon customization department comes from weapon tiering, which while keeping loot engaging into the later hours of the game, prevents many unique weapons (Fiscal Quarter comes to mind as an obvious example) from being useful at all, especially upon entering New Game+.

New Game+ is a first for a Bethesda RPG, and it adds a compelling source of replayability, allowing players to keep their skills while also being able to solve problems in different ways. Unfortunately, this isn't as compelling as it could be. The main story features little variance, and outside of a single choice at the end of the story, the only place where a choice actually felt significant was during the Crimson Fleet faction questline. 

Stealth gameplay saw a handful of improvements over previous Bethesda RPGs. The Ryujin Industries questline is entirely based around stealth and espionage, and even killing enemies is frowned upon. To enable more effective stealth, non-lethal options are available for many energy weapons, allowing enemies to be incapacitated instead of outright killed. Additionally, limited invisibility effects and stealth chems are featured, alongside a number of skills that enhance stealth capabilities. Level design for stealth-specific quests is also regularly very good, featuring security cameras to avoid or destroy and occasional disguises.

Dialog is fun, but only sometimes. Skills, traits, and your character's background can open additional dialog, which allows for certain persuasion challenges to be skipped, or for additional resources or information to be provided. The persuasion challenges have been expanded to full minigames, where you need to select the right options to win over your target, each of which will slowly chip away at convincing them.

Smuggling is technically a feature of the video game, and that's all I have to say about it.

Ship customization is fun, though cargo capacity can be a bit annoying early on. My final ship ended up being a behemoth with automatic particle turrets, 4500 cargo capacity, and ten entire landing legs. Money becomes no obstacle as the story progresses, allowing the ship customization to truly open itself to you, and I truly believe that in a different game this system would be really good. Alas, it isn't, and so it feels mostly like a novelty.

Basebuilding is back, and this time you don't have to spend like thirty dollars for all of the building items. It's fine. There's an achievement for connecting five bases with cargo links, and it made me want to pull out my hair, but otherwise it's an interesting enough system.

The story is decent, but it takes a while to get good. I thoroughly believe that Entangled and Unearthed are two of the best quests I have ever played in a Bethesda RPG, but they're buried underneath a heap of "go here, clear a dungeon, nab an artifact" so most players don't get to experience them. The dawning realization of the twist during Unearthed was the height of my experience with this game.

Creations are back, and I think they're just okay. I like them conceptually, but I know other people don't so I won't say much beyond that they're community-made mods, some of which you can spend money on to support the creator and enable achievements when playing with them. I used a few in my time, and they weren't anything particularly special.

Scale is a bit too much in my opinion. 120 solar systems, averaging like eight planets and moons, each with their own environments and locations, most of which are cookie-cutter dungeons procedurally generated from a list. After a certain point, the only reason to go places outside of quests is for specific organic and inorganic resources, which really takes the wind out of my sails because I like exploring in these games.

Overall, a solid 6.5/10 with some staying power. Lots of missed opportunities, lots of confusing systems, and lots of potential fun buried in the noise. The DLC is like a 7.5/10, but suffers from many of the same problems. Send post.
